title: The Stations of the Cross
hook: fourteen stops from condemnation to the tomb

segments.voice: Yesterday, almsgiving, and Lent's three practices. Your line was in secret. Did you manage not to tell anyone? Day one hundred fifty.

Fourteen small pictures or carvings hang along the side walls of many Catholic churches, evenly spaced, each with a little cross above it and a Roman numeral underneath. Most weeks nobody pays them much attention. But on Friday evenings in Lent, the lights dim and a small group gathers at the first one. They stand. They kneel. They move to the next. Slowly, the whole group walks the walls of the church, all the way around, until they end at the tomb. Today: the stations.
screen: `FOURTEEN PICTURES ON THE WALLS.` → `FRIDAY EVENINGS IN LENT.` → `ALL THE WAY AROUND.`

segments.voice: The Stations of the Cross, also called the Way of the Cross, are fourteen stops on Jesus's last journey: from Pilate condemning him, through carrying the cross, the crucifixion, and finally his body laid in the tomb. The word station comes from the Latin statio, a standing place, a place where you stop. It started in Jerusalem, where for centuries pilgrims walked the road Christians believed Jesus walked, praying where things happened. That road is called the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrow. Few Christians could travel to Jerusalem, so over the Middle Ages, and especially through the Franciscans, who looked after the holy places, the walk was brought home. Churches set up stopping points so anyone could make the pilgrimage in their own parish. The number fourteen was settled in the eighteenth century. It's honest to say that some stations come straight from the Gospels, like Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross, and Jesus speaking to the women of Jerusalem. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Others come from tradition: Jesus falling three times, meeting his mother on the way, and Veronica wiping his face. The Gospels don't describe those. In 1991, Pope John Paul the Second led a version with stations drawn only from Scripture, and both forms are prayed today. At each station, people often say, we adore you, O Christ, and we praise you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world. Then a reading, a reflection, a prayer, and on to the next. The aim is not to watch, but to walk with him.
screen: `FOURTEEN STOPS TO THE TOMB.` · `STATIO: A PLACE TO STOP.` · `JERUSALEM, BROUGHT HOME.` · `SOME FROM GOSPELS, SOME TRADITION.` · then, large: `WEEP NOT OVER ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly and stop three times. If you can, stand up and take a few slow steps across the room. If you can't, do this in your imagination. Settle, and breathe. First stop: Jesus takes up the cross. Pause. Think of something heavy you're carrying. Walk a little. Second stop: Simon helps him. Think of someone who has helped you carry something. Walk a little. Third stop: he meets the women of Jerusalem. Think of someone who is grieving. If you pray, pray at each stop. The bell holds the time.
Stations. From the Latin for a place to stop. Fourteen stops on Jesus's road from condemnation to the tomb, walked around the walls of a church. Today's word.

Your line: walk it with him. Today, when you walk anywhere, stop three times for one breath, and think of someone carrying something heavy. Tomorrow, the three holiest days begin. Day one hundred fifty.

notes: Fourteen stations fixed in the 18th century (Clement XII, 1731; Benedict XIV, 1742); earlier numbers varied. Confirm.
Franciscan custody of the Holy Land (from 1342) and role in spreading the devotion; Leonard of Port Maurice not named. Confirm.
The response 'We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you...' is traditional; wording varies. Said without quotation marks. Confirm.
Traditional stations not in the Gospels: falls (3, 7, 9), meeting his mother (4), Veronica (6). Confirm.
